title: Can Deterministic Network Verification Reduce Undetected Faults in LLM‑Generated Configurations?
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (study id c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001) to measure whether inserting a deterministic network verifier between an LLM intent→configuration generator and an emulated execution reduces the proportion of configurations that would execute with operational faults. Using shared_initial_candidate semantics (one identical LLM candidate per intent evaluated both without and with verification), we evaluated 72 preregistered paired intents with gpt-5-mini and a canonical deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution completed with 144 episodes (72 pairs) and 72 model calls. All baseline executions produced no emulator-observed faults (n_11 = 72, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0). The paired difference in undetected-fault proportion is 0.0 (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.0, 0.0], exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; bootstrap seed = 1729, resamples = 10000). Under shared_initial_candidate semantics this degenerate confirmatory outcome is expected when identical generated candidates produce no baseline execution faults. We provide full preregistration rationale, deterministic execution accounting, representative validator traces, exact inferential outputs, and concrete methodological recommendations to measure verifier utility under realistic error regimes (independent-generation arms, repair-enabled flows, adversarial task sets).

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate high-level operator intents into low-level device configurations for network operations (NetOps). This intent→configuration translation promises faster change pipelines but raises operational risk: a generated configuration can silently violate reachability, security policy, or dependency-ordering invariants and cause outages if executed without further checks. A practical mitigation in deployment proposals is a generate–verify–repair (GVR) architecture that pairs stochastic LLM generation with deterministic verification and, when needed, repair or human review. Prior work demonstrates promising intent→configuration accuracy in constrained vendor dialects [1] and prototype co-pilots that include verification components [2], but systematic, preregistered experiments that report verifier detection performance against executed outcomes remain scarce [3].

This paper reports a preregistered, paired experiment that isolates the verifier’s detection capability on identical generator outputs under shared_initial_candidate semantics. The central research question is: does inserting a deterministic network verifier between an LLM generator and emulator execution materially reduce the proportion of configurations that execute with operational faults when the identical generated candidate is evaluated both without and with verification? We emphasize that, by design, the experiment does not measure benefits arising from alternative generator samples or repair-enabled iterations; instead it measures pure detection on the same candidate, avoiding confounding due to generator sampling variability. Our empirical contribution is an artifact-grounded, fully archived confirmatory run (72 paired intents) showing a degenerate ceiling outcome (zero baseline faults), plus a careful methodological analysis describing why that outcome follows from the preregistered contract and how future confirmatory designs should be specified to measure operational verifier utility.
sections.related_work:
Several recent studies explore LLM-based intent→configuration translation and NetOps co-pilots. Nguyen et al. demonstrated intent-based configuration generation with constrained vendor dialects and measured task-level accuracy in emulator-based evaluations [1]. Multi-agent and tool-augmented frameworks for intent-driven NetOps have been proposed and prototyped; these systems often integrate validators to reduce regressions but typically lack preregistered detection-evaluation against emulator-executed outcomes [2,4]. The generate–verify–repair architecture has precedent in code-generation and software-repair research, where deterministic checkers and test suites are used to validate and iteratively repair stochastic outputs; these systems motivate a similar stack for network configurations but adaptation to network semantics and runtime execution effects requires domain-specific evaluation [3].

Classical deterministic network verification techniques (header-space analysis, policy checkers, and related reachability analyses) are natural verifier candidates for NetOps GVR stacks because they provide precise invariants such as reachability, ACL behavior, and ordering constraints under a modeled forwarding plane [5]. Our study situates a preregistered paired test—focused on verifier detection on identical candidates—within this literature and explicitly avoids claiming general GVR benefits that require repair-orchestrated or independent-generation designs.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. We preregistered study c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001 and froze the design and analysis before observing outcomes. The primary estimand is the paired reduction in undetected operational-fault proportion (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline). The confirmatory hypothesis H1 targeted a paired absolute reduction of 0.20 with alpha = 0.05 and power ≥ 0.80; the preregistered sample size was N = 72 pairs stratified equally across three topology-difficulty strata.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and experimental contract. Per the execution_contract, each intent received exactly one initial LLM generation (shared across baseline and guarded conditions). Baseline: the shared candidate is executed in an isolated emulator and the outcome (fault/no fault) is recorded. Guarded: the deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) is run on the same candidate; if it flags violations the guarded outcome is recorded as prevented (no emulator execution); if it does not flag, the identical candidate is executed. This contract isolates verifier detection on identical outputs and prevents generator-sampling differences from influencing the paired comparison. Importantly, because only one shared candidate exists per intent, the verifier cannot improve outcomes by prompting or producing alternate candidates in the guarded arm—only deterministic detection and the prevention policy can affect the paired outcome.

Model, adapter, and verifier. The recorded model configuration (execution/model_configuration.json) declares requested_model = gpt-5-mini and provider = openai_responses; runtime sampling used the provider default (temperature recorded as null in the archived configuration). The adapter family was hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and the canonical verifier was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = "5.0"). The verifier implements a full_intent_constraint_validation rule set that produces a binary per-episode validity outcome and a structured validator_trace containing parsed_command_count, required_command_count, validation_before/after states, normalized_configuration, violation_codes, and a difficulty metadata object.

Task-bank construction, contamination controls, and difficulty strata. Tasks were generated deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Each task manifest entry includes: explicit natural-language intent, required_sequence (ordered field changes), allowed_touched_fields, initial and expected final states, and structured difficulty labels (medium/hard/very_hard) and patterns (e.g., make_before_break, shutdown_configure_restore). Exact-match contamination checks against public corpora were applied per preregistration; any exact-match would trigger exclusion from confirmatory analysis. In the executed run no confirmatory pairs were excluded.

Execution protocol, retry policy, and deterministic accounting. The missingness_plan allowed up to two additional retries for transient hosted-API errors; retries and all provider-call metadata were logged. The execution manifest records completed_episode_count = 144 (72 pairs × 2 conditions), failed_episode_count = 0, and model_calls_used = 72 (one shared generation per pair). Provider call audit in deterministic_reconciliation.json records hosted_model_call_event_count = 72, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 72, cache_miss_count = 72, and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 72}.

Scoring and statistical analysis. The verifier yields episode-level binary outcomes (valid vs violation) and detailed traces. The primary analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1 to construct the paired contingency table and apply an exact McNemar two-sided test where discordant pairs exist. We computed paired bootstrap percentile 95% confidence intervals for the paired difference with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap seed = 1729) to provide reproducible uncertainty quantification. Pre-specified subgroup confirmatory comparisons (topology complexity and policy type) were included in the preregistration with Holm correction; given the observed null/ceiling outcome these subgroup tests remain non-informative in this dataset.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting. The run completed without technical failures. Key deterministic artifact counts (from deterministic_reconciliation.json and execution manifest): planned_episode_count = 144; completed_episode_count = 144; failed_episode_count = 0; model_calls_used = 72. Provider-call accounting shows completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 72 and cache_miss_count = 72, consistent with one independent shared generation per pair.

Paired contingency and inferential outcomes. Aggregating across the 72 preregistered pairs yields contingency counts n_11 = 72, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0 (guarded × baseline). The paired estimate paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline = 0.0. The exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI computed with 10,000 resamples (seed = 1729) is [0.0, 0.0], reflecting the degenerate distribution produced by the absence of discordant pairs. Per-condition summaries (analysis/condition_summary.csv) record baseline success_rate = 1.0 and guarded success_rate = 1.0. All numerical analysis outputs, the contingency CSV, and the analysis log are archived in analysis/* artifacts and reproduce with the archived bootstrap seed.

Representative validator traces and diagnostics. Representative scoring artifacts (execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json through task-000006-*.json) show that deterministic_netops_validator_v5 parsed and validated required command sequences for each shared candidate. Example validator_trace fields present in the archived JSON for each episode include: parsed_command_count (range 2–6), required_command_count, difficulty.level (medium/hard/very_hard), normalized_configuration, validation_before and validation_after final_state mappings, validator_version = "5.0", score_reason_code = "VALID_CONFIGURATION", and violation_count = 0 for the sampled examples. These traces confirm the verifier executed and produced no violation flags on the generated candidates in the preregistered task bank.

Contamination, exclusions, and missingness. analysis/contamination_summary.csv records zero flagged exact-match contaminations for confirmatory pairs. analysis/missingness_summary.csv records complete_pairs = 72 and zero failed or unscorable episodes across conditions. The absence of exclusions or failures simplifies interpretation but produces a ceiling effect that eliminates the possibility of detecting verifier benefit in this paired contract.

Sensitivity checks. Pre-specified sensitivity analyses (treating excluded pairs as failures; bootstrap diagnostics) were executable with the archived artifacts. Because there were no excluded pairs and no discordant outcomes, these sensitivity analyses yield the same degenerate numerical conclusion (paired difference = 0.0). The reproducible bootstrap setup (seed = 1729, resamples = 10000) is recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl and produces the reported CI collapse to a point mass.
sections.discussion:
Confirmatory interpretation and causes of the ceiling outcome. The preregistered paired design with shared_initial_candidate semantics validly measures verifier detection on identical candidates. Observing zero baseline faults yields a scientifically informative ceiling/null outcome: under the chosen model (gpt-5-mini), prompt/template, and synthetic task bank the generator outputs were uniformly valid in the emulator and thus the verifier had no executed failures to prevent. The numeric outputs (n_11 = 72, p = 1.0, bootstrap CI [0.0, 0.0]) are direct consequences of the preregistered contract and the observed data and are therefore not evidence that verifiers are unnecessary in general.

Design implications for future confirmatory tests. The shared_initial_candidate contract provides a clean isolation of verifier detection but sacrifices sensitivity to verifier-mediated benefits that arise through repairs or alternate candidate selection. To measure operational utility of verifiers in practice, future preregistered designs should include one or more of: (1) independent-generation arms that allow separate generator calls per condition (baseline vs guarded) so that verifier-triggered repairs or different sampling can change the executed candidate distribution; (2) repair-enabled flows where the verifier, upon flagging, triggers a single deterministic repair call and the repaired candidate is executed and assessed end-to-end; (3) adversarial or fault-injection task banks that intentionally increase baseline error prevalence (sequencing violations, ambiguous intents, protocol-specific edge cases) to reveal true positive and false positive tradeoffs; (4) multi-model and sampling-parameter sweeps to evaluate model- and sampling-sensitivity to verification performance.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: the single shared generation per intent and provider-default sampling (temperature recorded as null) introduce runtime sampling semantics that are recorded but not experimentally varied. Construct validity: emulator-observed faults are a conservative proxy for operational harm but do not capture traffic-dependent, timing, or cross-device emergent failures present in production. External validity: experiments used one declared model (gpt-5-mini), a synthetic/emulated task bank, and one deterministic verifier; extrapolation to other models, vendor dialects, or production hardware is not supported. Conclusion validity: because baseline error prevalence was zero for the preregistered task bank, the confirmatory design has no power to demonstrate verifier benefit in this execution.

Operational implications. The observed absence of baseline faults suggests that under constrained prompts, dialects, and emulator settings, modern LLMs can produce high task-level accuracy. This finding should not be generalized to production operations. Organizations should treat deterministic verifiers as part of layered risk control; demonstrating a verifier’s operational utility requires experiments that produce non-negligible baseline error rates or permit repair-mediated improvements.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired evaluation (study id c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001) under shared_initial_candidate semantics to measure whether a canonical deterministic verifier reduces the proportion of LLM‑generated configurations that would execute with operational faults. For the chosen model (gpt-5-mini), verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and synthetic/emulated task bank, baseline executions produced zero emulator faults and the verifier did not change outcomes (paired difference = 0.0, bootstrap 95% CI [0.0, 0.0], exact McNemar p = 1.0). This artifact-grounded null/ceiling outcome is internally consistent with the preregistered design: when identical generated candidates produce no executed faults, a verifier cannot reduce executed faults under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Measuring verifier utility under realistic error regimes requires experimental contracts that permit independent or multiple generator samples, repair-enabled flows, adversarial task sets, and multi-model comparisons. All execution artifacts, validator traces, and analysis logs referenced here are archived in the evidence bundle to support replication and targeted follow-on studies.

Models and tools: initial generation used gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version recorded in execution/model_configuration.json) orchestrated via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter; deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = "5.0") served as the canonical verifier; an isolated emulator executed candidate configurations. Preregistration: study c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001 was preregistered and frozen before observing outcomes. Execution artifacts and deterministic analysis logs (execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, deterministic_reconciliation.json, and others) are archived in the registered evidence bundle and contain the authoritative recorded model configuration (including temperature = null), provider call audit counts, and validator traces. No human manual manuscript editing or content insertion occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Confirmatory ceiling/null outcome: baseline generator produced zero emulator faults on the preregistered task set, preventing direct measurement of verifier detection benefit.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the design measures verifier effect on the same generated candidate only and does not assess independent per‑condition generation, multi‑sample generation, or repairs unless explicitly permitted by the contract.
Single‑model scope: experiments used one declared model (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across models or versions.
Synthetic/emulated tasks: task corpus and emulator executions differ from production devices and live traffic; external validity to production deployments is limited.

Sampling‑parameter uncertainty: execution/model_configuration.json shows temperature = null (sampling parameters unset); null indicates provider default sampling semantics determined runtime sampling behavior and is a residual uncertainty recorded in the archived configuration.

Residual contamination risk: deterministic provenance and exact‑match checks were applied, but private training‑data contamination of the hosted model cannot be fully ruled out and remains residual uncertainty.
